--- title: "Logistic regression with two binary predictors" format: html: df-print: kable toc: true toc-depth: 3 number-sections: true --- # Two predictors in additive and multiplicative models The previous logistic regression chapters considered one predictor at a time. Clinical questions often ask whether a treatment contrast looks different in a baseline subgroup. Here we model the probability of a **treatment response** using: - treatment group (`trt`); and - a binary baseline PHQ-9 category (`phq_cat`). Our research question is: > Within each PHQ-9 category, how does the estimated probability of treatment response differ between therapist-guided treatment and waitlist? We will first fit an additive logistic model and then a model with `trt * phq_cat`. Results will be presented using the probability difference, log-odds and odds ratios. # Packages and data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(here) library(broom) library(marginaleffects) options( marginaleffects_print_omit = c("s.value"), marginaleffects_print_style = ifelse(interactive(), "summary", "tinytable") ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df_binary <- read_csv2(here("data", "steps_clean.csv")) |> filter(!is.na(lsas_screen), !is.na(lsas_post)) |> mutate( # The second outcome level is the event modeled by binomial glm(). lsas_response = factor( if_else( (lsas_screen - lsas_post) / lsas_screen >= 0.30, "Response", "No response" ), levels = c("No response", "Response") ), trt = factor( trt, levels = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided", "self-guided") ), phq_cat = factor( case_when( phq9_screen < 10 ~ "< 10", phq9_screen >= 10 ~ ">= 10" ), levels = c("< 10", ">= 10") ) ) |> filter(trt %in% c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")) |> droplevels() df_binary |> count(phq_cat, lsas_response, .drop = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|phq_cat |lsas_response | n| |:-------|:-------------|--:| |< 10 |No response | 40| |< 10 |Response | 21| |>= 10 |No response | 35| |>= 10 |Response | 16|
::: ::: `phq_cat` explicitly divides baseline PHQ-9 scores into `< 10` and `>= 10`. It is a convenient binary moderator for this lesson. [Logistic regression with a binary and numeric predictor](logistic-binary-numeric-predictors.qmd) keeps PHQ-9 continuous. The outcome is treatment response, defined as a reduction of at least 30% from baseline LSAS. Waitlist is the reference treatment group, `< 10` is the reference PHQ-9 category, and `Response` is the modeled outcome event. # Additive logistic model An additive model has treatment and PHQ-9-category terms but no product term: $$ \operatorname{logit}\left[P(Y_i = \mathrm{Response})\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 trt_i + \beta_2 phq_i $$ On the **log-odds scale**, this model says that the treatment odds ratio is the same in both PHQ-9 categories. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_additive <- glm( lsas_response ~ trt + phq_cat, family = binomial, data = df_binary ) summary(mod_additive) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = lsas_response ~ trt + phq_cat, family = binomial, data = df_binary) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -2.14895 0.48573 -4.424 9.68e-06 *** trttherapist-guided 2.45679 0.51206 4.798 1.60e-06 *** phq_cat>= 10 -0.02193 0.46766 -0.047 0.963 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1) Null deviance: 142.11 on 111 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 112.25 on 109 degrees of freedom AIC: 118.25 Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4 ``` ::: ::: We can get the ORs for therapist-guided versus waitlist and for PHQ-9 `>= 10` versus `< 10` by exponentiating the coefficients. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} b_additive <- coef(mod_additive) exp(b_additive[["trttherapist-guided"]]) # OR therapist-guided vs waitlist ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 11.66727 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} exp(b_additive[["phq_cat>= 10"]]) # OR PHQ-9 >= 10 vs < 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9783106 ``` ::: ::: The fact that the odds ratio is the same in both PHQ-9 categories does *not* guarantee identical probability differences: changing a probability by a fixed odds ratio can produce different percentage-point changes at different baseline probabilities. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} additive_probabilities <- predictions( mod_additive, newdata = datagrid(trt = unique, phq_cat = unique) ) additive_treatment_effects <- avg_comparisons( mod_additive, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), by = "phq_cat", type = "response" ) additive_treatment_low_phq <- additive_treatment_effects |> filter(phq_cat == "< 10") additive_treatment_high_phq <- additive_treatment_effects |> filter(phq_cat == ">= 10") additive_odds_ratio <- tidy( mod_additive, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE ) |> filter(term == "trttherapist-guided") additive_probabilities ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
trt phq_cat Estimate Pr(>|z|) 2.5 % 97.5 %
Type: invlink(link)
waitlist < 10 0.104 <0.001 0.0431 0.232
waitlist >= 10 0.102 <0.001 0.0414 0.231
therapist-guided < 10 0.576 0.365 0.4113 0.726
therapist-guided >= 10 0.571 0.457 0.3853 0.739
``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} additive_treatment_effects ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
phq_cat Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) 2.5 % 97.5 %
Term: trt
Comparison: therapist-guided - waitlist
Type: response
< 10 0.472 0.0832 5.68 <0.001 0.309 0.635
>= 10 0.469 0.0894 5.24 <0.001 0.293 0.644
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Model interpretation Compared with waitlist, therapist-guided treatment has an estimated probability of treatment response that is **higher by 47.2 percentage points** among participants with baseline PHQ-9 `< 10` (95% CI **30.9 to 63.5 percentage points**). Among participants with baseline PHQ-9 `>= 10`, it is **higher by 46.9 percentage points** (95% CI **29.3 to 64.4 percentage points**). Because this is an additive *logistic* model, its therapist-guided-versus-waitlist odds ratio is **11.67** (95% CI **4.53 to 34.62**) in both PHQ-9 categories, adjusted for PHQ-9 category. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_predictions( mod_additive, condition = c("trt", "phq_cat") ) + labs( title = "Additive logistic model", subtitle = "Probabilities by treatment and baseline PHQ-9 category", x = "Treatment group", y = "Estimated probability of treatment response (95% CI)", color = "Baseline PHQ-9" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Additive-model estimated probabilities of treatment response. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals.](logistic-two-binary-predictors_files/figure-html/plot-additive-probabilities-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: # Interaction model ::: callout-note ## Effect modification, interaction, and moderation These terms are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things. - **Effect modification**: the effect of one intervention (here, treatment) differs across levels of another variable (here, baseline PHQ-9 category). Only the first variable needs to be something we could intervene on; the second is a characteristic we condition on [@VanderWeele2009Interaction]. - **Causal interaction**: the effect of intervening on *both* variables together differs from what their separate effects would imply. Both variables must be things we could, at least in principle, intervene on [@VanderWeele2009Interaction]. - **Moderation**: the term most used in psychology for a variable that changes the direction or strength of a relationship [@Baron1986Moderator]. In randomized trials, @Kraemer2002Moderators define a moderator as a characteristic measured before randomization, and therefore unrelated to treatment, that identifies subgroups with different treatment effects. This is close to effect modification. Treatment is randomized, but PHQ-9 is not, so this chapter studies effect modification. We can estimate whether the treatment effect differs between PHQ-9 categories, but not what would happen if we changed a participant's depression, and a difference between the categories may reflect other characteristics that go with higher PHQ-9 scores. All three depend on the scale. A model can show no interaction on one scale and an interaction on another [@VanderWeele2014Tutorial]. The additive model above is an example: it has no interaction on the log-odds scale, yet its probability differences differ between the PHQ-9 categories (47.2 versus 46.9 percentage points). Here the difference is tiny because PHQ-9 category barely predicts response (odds ratio 0.98), so both categories start from almost the same probability under waitlist. With baseline PHQ-9 kept continuous, the probability difference in the additive model changes visibly across scores; see [logistic regression with a binary and numeric predictor](logistic-binary-numeric-predictors.qmd). When you report effect modification, name the scale, for example the probability difference (an additive scale) or the odds ratio (a multiplicative scale). ::: The interaction model adds a product term, written `trt * phq_cat` in the model formula: $$ \operatorname{logit}\left[P(Y_i = \mathrm{Response})\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 trt_i + \beta_2 phq_i + \beta_3(trt_i \times phq_i). $$ The product term lets the treatment association with the outcome differ by baseline PHQ-9 category. Because both predictors are indicators (0/1), the product $trt_i \times phq_i$ equals 1 only for therapist-guided participants with PHQ-9 `>= 10`, so $\beta_3$ applies to that group alone. The treatment coefficient $\beta_1$ is now the treatment log-odds difference in the reference category, PHQ-9 `< 10`; it is not an overall treatment effect. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_interaction <- glm( lsas_response ~ trt * phq_cat, family = binomial, data = df_binary ) summary(mod_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = lsas_response ~ trt * phq_cat, family = binomial, data = df_binary) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -2.19722 0.60853 -3.611 0.000305 *** trttherapist-guided 2.52265 0.70908 3.558 0.000374 *** phq_cat>= 10 0.07696 0.86233 0.089 0.928885 trttherapist-guided:phq_cat>= 10 -0.14002 1.02617 -0.136 0.891466 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1) Null deviance: 142.11 on 111 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 112.23 on 108 degrees of freedom AIC: 120.23 Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4 ``` ::: ::: We can exponentiate the coefficients to express them on the odds-ratio scale. In an interaction model, however, the treatment coefficient now represents the treatment effect when PHQ-9 is in its reference category (`< 10`). Thus, $\exp(\beta_1)$ is the OR for therapist-guided treatment versus waitlist among participants with PHQ-9 `< 10`. The interaction coefficient tells us how the treatment OR changes when moving from PHQ-9 `< 10` to PHQ-9 `>= 10`. Here, $\exp(\beta_3)$ is the ratio of the two treatment ORs. To obtain the treatment OR among participants with PHQ-9 `>= 10`, we therefore combine the treatment and interaction coefficients: $\exp(\beta_1 + \beta_3)$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} b_interaction <- coef(mod_interaction) b1 <- b_interaction[["trttherapist-guided"]] b3 <- b_interaction[["trttherapist-guided:phq_cat>= 10"]] exp(b1) # treatment OR when PHQ-9 < 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 12.46154 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} exp(b3) # ratio of treatment ORs ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.8693416 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} exp(b1 + b3) # treatment OR when PHQ-9 >= 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 10.83333 ``` ::: ::: To go from the odds scale to the probability scale, we can again use functions from the `marginaleffects` package: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} interaction_probabilities <- predictions( mod_interaction, newdata = datagrid(trt = unique, phq_cat = unique) ) interaction_probabilities ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
trt phq_cat Estimate Pr(>|z|) 2.5 % 97.5 %
Type: invlink(link)
waitlist < 10 0.100 <0.001 0.0326 0.268
waitlist >= 10 0.107 <0.001 0.0350 0.284
therapist-guided < 10 0.581 0.371 0.4042 0.739
therapist-guided >= 10 0.565 0.533 0.3631 0.748
``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} interaction_treatment_effects <- avg_comparisons( mod_interaction, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), by = "phq_cat", type = "response" ) interaction_treatment_effects ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
phq_cat Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) 2.5 % 97.5 %
Term: trt
Comparison: therapist-guided - waitlist
Type: response
< 10 0.481 0.104 4.61 <0.001 0.276 0.685
>= 10 0.458 0.119 3.86 <0.001 0.225 0.691
``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Model interpretation Within the baseline PHQ-9 `< 10` category, therapist-guided treatment has an estimated probability of treatment response that is **higher by 48.1 percentage points** than waitlist (95% CI **27.6 to 68.5 percentage points**). Within the baseline PHQ-9 `>= 10` category, the corresponding probability is **higher by 45.8 percentage points** (95% CI **22.5 to 69.1 percentage points**). The associated therapist-guided-versus-waitlist odds ratios are **12.46** (95% CI **3.10 to 50.02**) for PHQ-9 `< 10` and **10.83** (95% CI **2.53 to 46.36**) for PHQ-9 `>= 10`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} interaction_probabilities |> ggplot(aes(x = trt, y = estimate, group = phq_cat, color = phq_cat)) + geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.1)) + geom_line(position = position_dodge(width = 0.1)) + geom_errorbar( aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.1, position = position_dodge(width = 0.1) ) + labs( title = "Interaction logistic model", subtitle = "Treatment probabilities may differ by baseline PHQ-9 category", x = "Treatment group", y = "Estimated probability of treatment response (95% CI)", color = "Baseline PHQ-9" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Interaction-model estimated probabilities of treatment response. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals.](logistic-two-binary-predictors_files/figure-html/plot-interaction-probabilities-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_comparisons( mod_interaction, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), by = "phq_cat", type = "response" ) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs( title = "Conditional treatment effects on the probability scale", x = "Baseline PHQ-9 category", y = "Therapist-guided minus waitlist probability difference (95% CI)" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Conditional therapist-guided-minus-waitlist probability differences from the interaction model. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals.](logistic-two-binary-predictors_files/figure-html/plot-conditional-treatment-effects-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Do the two probability differences differ? It might be tempting to compare the two intervals in the plot by eye. But overlapping intervals, or one interval excluding zero while the other does not, do not tell us whether the two treatment effects differ [@Gelman2006Difference]. To answer that question, estimate the difference between the two probability differences directly. `hypothesis = difference ~ reference` subtracts the first row of the comparisons, the reference PHQ-9 category `< 10`, from each other row, here PHQ-9 `>= 10`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} interaction_rd_difference <- avg_comparisons( mod_interaction, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), by = "phq_cat", type = "response", hypothesis = difference ~ reference ) interaction_rd_difference ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) 2.5 % 97.5 %
Type: response
(>= 10) - (< 10) -0.0226 0.158 -0.143 0.886 -0.332 0.287
``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Ratio of treatment ORs: PHQ-9 >= 10 divided by PHQ-9 < 10 interaction_or_ratio <- tidy( mod_interaction, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE ) |> filter(term == "trttherapist-guided:phq_cat>= 10") interaction_or_ratio ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| conf.low| conf.high| |:--------------------------------|---------:|---------:|----------:|---------:|---------:|---------:| |trttherapist-guided:phq_cat>= 10 | 0.8693416| 1.026166| -0.1364489| 0.8914664| 0.1110342| 6.814128|
::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Model interpretation The therapist-guided-minus-waitlist probability difference is **2.3 percentage points smaller** among participants with baseline PHQ-9 `>= 10` than among those with PHQ-9 `< 10` (95% CI **-33.2** to **28.7 percentage points**). This is the interaction on the probability scale: a difference between two probability differences. The interval is wide enough to include large differences in either direction, so these data cannot tell us whether the treatment effect differs between the PHQ-9 categories. On the odds-ratio scale, the treatment OR for PHQ-9 `>= 10` divided by the treatment OR for PHQ-9 `< 10` is **0.87** (95% CI **0.11** to **6.81**). ::: ::: callout-caution ## Interaction tests need large samples Effect modification is estimated from the smallest cells of the design. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} interaction_cell_counts <- df_binary |> count(trt, phq_cat, lsas_response) |> pivot_wider(names_from = lsas_response, values_from = n) interaction_cell_counts ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|trt |phq_cat | No response| Response| |:----------------|:-------|-----------:|--------:| |waitlist |< 10 | 27| 3| |waitlist |>= 10 | 25| 3| |therapist-guided |< 10 | 13| 18| |therapist-guided |>= 10 | 10| 13|
::: ::: In the waitlist arm, only 3 participants responded in the PHQ-9 `< 10` category and 3 in the `>= 10` category. Estimates based on so few events are unstable, and a cell with no events at all would leave the model unable to estimate its log-odds (a problem known as separation). More generally, an interaction needs far more data than a main effect of the same size: roughly four times the sample size in a two-arm trial with equally sized subgroups [@Brookes2004Subgroup]. A trial powered for its overall treatment effect is therefore rarely powered to detect effect modification, and a non-significant interaction is weak evidence that none exists. ::: # Interpreting the interaction An interaction model can describe different conditional estimates, but it does not automatically establish a clinically meaningful subgroup. Before presenting a subgroup finding, ask: 1. Were the moderator and the interaction planned before looking at the data? 2. Are the conditional probability differences precise enough to distinguish meaningful patterns from sampling variation? 3. Does the interaction plot show a consistent, clinically interpretable pattern rather than an isolated coefficient or p-value? 4. Would the conclusion be different if PHQ-9 were modeled continuously? See [logistic regression with a binary and numeric predictor](logistic-binary-numeric-predictors.qmd). The interaction coefficient is a difference of **log-odds contrasts**. It is not itself the difference between the two probability differences; that difference is the `hypothesis` estimate above. `avg_comparisons()` gives the quantities we want to communicate: therapist-guided-minus-waitlist probability differences within the explicitly stated PHQ-9 categories. # Summary In this chapter you learned to: - derive `phq_cat` explicitly as baseline PHQ-9 `< 10` versus `>= 10`; - fit additive and `trt * phq_cat` binary logistic models with `glm(..., family = binomial)`; - report treatment contrasts as conditional probability differences in percentage points with 95% CIs; - distinguish a conditional odds ratio from a probability difference; - distinguish effect modification, causal interaction, and moderation, and name the scale on which effect modification is assessed; - estimate the difference between two conditional probability differences directly, and explain why interaction tests need large samples; and - use predicted-probability and conditional-effect plots to inspect a proposed subgroup pattern.
